item.content:encoded:
The International Detention Coalition (IDC) is inviting qualified professionals to apply for the position of Europe Programme Officer – Balkans, a full-time remote programme management role supporting migration, human rights, advocacy, research, communications, stakeholder engagement and regional programming across the Western Balkans and wider Europe.

The position offers an annual salary of EUR 30,000 to EUR 40,000, depending on the candidate’s location and experience, and is offered initially on a one-year contract with the possibility of extension depending on funding. The role is remote-first, although office-based or co-working arrangements may be available in some countries.

Candidates must already have the legal right to reside and work in one of the specified countries: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia. The organization states that it cannot sponsor work permits or provide relocation support.

The application deadline is 16 October 2026.

About the International Detention Coalition

The International Detention Coalition is a global network comprising more than 200 civil society organizations and individuals across more than 75 countries. The organization works with members and partners on advocacy, research, coalition building and capacity strengthening with the aim of eliminating immigration detention and advancing rights-based alternatives to detention.

IDC’s work involves collaboration with a broad range of actors, including civil society organizations, governments, decision-makers, UN agencies, regional institutions, community groups and people with lived experience.

The organization describes its approach as solutions-focused and emphasizes working with different stakeholders to develop alternatives that benefit migrants, communities and wider society.

The Europe Programme Officer – Balkans will therefore join an organization working at the intersection of migration, asylum, human rights, advocacy, policy, research and regional cooperation.

Europe Programme Officer – Balkans Job Overview

The Europe Programme Officer – Balkans will support IDC’s mission in the Balkans and contribute to the organization’s broader Europe programme.

The position involves working closely with the Europe Regional Manager and other IDC colleagues to support regional programmes, advocacy strategies, events, research, communications and stakeholder engagement.

The successful candidate will also contribute to strengthening relationships with IDC members, partners, decision-makers, and other stakeholders across the Balkans and wider Europe.

The organization is looking for someone who is highly organized, motivated and experienced in migration and human rights advocacy, with a strong understanding of the Western Balkans context. Strong communication, planning, organizational and stakeholder engagement abilities are particularly important for the role.

Because the position covers regional programming, the successful candidate should also be prepared to travel when required.

Key Details of the Job

  • Job title: Europe Programme Officer – Balkans
  • Employer: International Detention Coalition
  • Department: Program Management
  • Employment type: Full-time
  • Work arrangement: Remote-first
  • Contract: One year, with possible extension depending on funding
  • Salary: EUR 30,000–40,000 per year, depending on location and experience
  • Reports to: Europe Regional Manager
  • Direct reports: Interns or volunteers where relevant; currently, the position has no direct reports
  • Location eligibility: Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia
  • Travel: Required as needed within the Balkans and wider Europe
  • Application language: English
  • Deadline: 16 October 2026

What Will the Europe Programme Officer – Balkans Do?

The position covers several interconnected areas, including programme implementation, administration, advocacy, stakeholder engagement, communications, research, monitoring, fundraising and institutional support.

1. Project Implementation and Programme Support

One of the central responsibilities will be supporting the implementation of national and regional projects and events across the Balkans, including Greece and the wider European programme.

The Programme Officer will provide technical, administrative and logistical support to the Europe Regional Programme while working collaboratively with relevant IDC staff and members.

Responsibilities include:

  • Supporting implementation of national and regional programmes.
  • Providing technical and administrative assistance for projects.
  • Supporting regional events and programme activities.
  • Helping implement IDC’s strategic priorities in Europe.
  • Supporting members and partners through network building and capacity strengthening.
  • Managing project timelines and deliverables.
  • Following up on agreed actions and deadlines.
  • Supporting financial and other administrative processes within the Europe Programme.

This means the position requires someone who can combine programme management and administrative coordination with advocacy and policy engagement.

2. Advocacy and Stakeholder Engagement

Advocacy is a major component of the position.

The Programme Officer will support the development and implementation of advocacy strategies addressing immigration detention, alternatives to detention, migrant rights and refugee rights, particularly within national contexts in the Balkans.

The role also involves supporting IDC’s engagement with the European Union and its institutions, particularly where EU migration and asylum policies intersect with Western Balkan accession and enlargement processes.

The successful candidate may therefore be expected to:

  • Monitor relevant EU migration and asylum policies.
  • Follow developments relating to EU enlargement and accession.
  • Contribute to national and regional advocacy strategies.
  • Support coordinated advocacy with civil society networks.
  • Engage with government representatives.
  • Work with local and regional civil society organizations.
  • Engage with UN agencies and regional institutions.
  • Develop relationships with relevant organizations and networks.
  • Help identify advocacy opportunities and policy gaps.

Strong stakeholder engagement skills will be important because the role requires coordination across government, civil society, international organizations and other regional actors.

3. Advocacy Communications and Policy Materials

The Programme Officer will also contribute to producing advocacy and communications materials.

This may include:

  • Advocacy documents.
  • Briefing notes.
  • Strategic communications.
  • Digital communications.
  • Materials for different stakeholder groups.
  • Social media content.
  • Information and resources for IDC members and partners.

The ability to communicate complex migration and human rights issues clearly to different audiences will therefore be valuable.

The role also includes helping disseminate resources among IDC members and monitoring relevant media platforms for developments in the Balkans and wider Europe.

4. Research, Data Collection and Evidence Gathering

Research is another important part of the position.

The Programme Officer will support research and evidence gathering related to:

  • Immigration detention.
  • Rights-based alternatives to detention.
  • Migration policy.
  • Human rights.
  • Regional developments.
  • National policy environments.
  • Advocacy opportunities.

The evidence collected will help inform IDC’s advocacy, communications and programme activities.

Candidates should therefore be comfortable conducting research, identifying relevant information, monitoring policy developments and translating evidence into useful programme or advocacy outputs.

5. Regional Networking and Partnership Building

The successful candidate will maintain regular contact with IDC members and partners across the Balkans and Europe.

This involves identifying:

  • Policy gaps.
  • Advocacy opportunities.
  • Potential partnerships.
  • Areas where members require support.
  • Opportunities for coordinated action.
  • Opportunities for regional dialogue.

The Programme Officer will also assist with planning and facilitating stakeholder consultations, trainings and regional events that promote rights-based alternatives, pathways and dialogue across the Balkans.

Experience working with networks and coalitions can therefore be particularly useful for this position.

6. Communications Responsibilities

The role includes practical communications responsibilities.

The Programme Officer will assist with developing print and digital communication materials for the Balkans, including social media content for different platforms.

The successful candidate will also:

  • Share resources with members through different communication platforms.
  • Monitor media platforms.
  • Track relevant reports and developments.
  • Support dissemination of information.
  • Contribute to communications around programme and advocacy activities.

This aspect of the position may be particularly relevant to professionals with experience in communications, public information, advocacy communications, digital media or strategic communications alongside migration or human rights work.

7. Monitoring, Evaluation and Learning

The Programme Officer will contribute to monitoring, evaluation and learning activities within the Europe Programme.

Responsibilities include supporting:

  • Accurate and timely monitoring.
  • Programme reporting.
  • Internal evaluation processes.
  • Donor accountability.
  • Documentation of project outcomes.
  • Tracking stakeholder engagement.
  • Recording communications activities.
  • Institutional knowledge management.

The role requires the successful candidate to maintain organized records and help ensure that programme information is available for internal learning, reporting and external dissemination.

Experience with MEL systems, reporting and documentation is therefore specifically relevant to the position.

8. Fundraising and Proposal Development

Fundraising is also included among the responsibilities.

The Programme Officer will actively contribute to IDC’s fundraising efforts by:

  • Conducting background research.
  • Identifying potential funders.
  • Coordinating contributions from relevant team members.
  • Supporting proposal development.
  • Helping ensure proposals align with Balkans and wider regional priorities.

The role may also involve budget tracking, planning and financial monitoring in collaboration with the Regional Manager, Executive Director and other relevant IDC colleagues.

Candidates with experience supporting donor proposals, fundraising research, grant applications, programme budgets, or donor reporting may therefore find this aspect of the position particularly relevant.

9. Teamwork, Safeguarding and Institutional Support

Beyond technical responsibilities, the Programme Officer is expected to contribute positively to IDC’s internal working culture.

The successful candidate will be expected to:

  • Promote collaboration and teamwork.
  • Support colleagues.
  • Demonstrate commitment to IDC’s mission and values.
  • Understand and follow relevant organizational policies.
  • Support safeguarding principles.
  • Engage with organizational systems and processes.
  • Help protect institutional knowledge and organizational assets.
  • Contribute to sustainable programme operations.

IDC highlights values including innovation, collaboration, respect, representation and being solutions-focused.

Essential Qualifications and Experience

Applicants should carefully review the essential selection criteria because the position requires a combination of academic qualifications, professional experience, regional knowledge and technical skills.

1. Knowledge of the European and Balkans Context

Applicants must demonstrate an understanding of the European context, particularly the Balkans and Greece, in relation to:

  • Migration.
  • Asylum.
  • Human rights.
  • Advocacy.
  • National policy.
  • Legislative processes.
  • Regional cooperation mechanisms.
  • EU accession processes.
  • EU enlargement processes.

This is one of the most important requirements because the role is specifically focused on the Balkans.

2. Advocacy and Government Engagement Experience

Candidates must have direct experience with advocacy or engagement involving:

  • Governments.
  • Institutions.
  • Civil society organizations.
  • EU institutions.

Relevant experience should relate to areas such as

  • Migration.
  • Asylum.
  • EU enlargement.
  • Related policy processes.

3. University Degree

Applicants must have a university degree in a relevant discipline.

Examples listed by IDC include:

  • International relations.
  • Law.
  • Migration studies.
  • Political science.
  • Social sciences.
  • An equivalent relevant field.

4. Minimum Three Years of Professional Experience

The position requires a minimum of three years of professional experience.

Relevant experience should include areas such as:

  • Project coordination.
  • Stakeholder engagement.
  • Advocacy.
  • Migration.
  • Human rights.
  • Work relevant to the Balkans.

5. Reporting, MEL, and Stakeholder Engagement

Applicants should demonstrate experience in:

  • Reporting.
  • Monitoring.
  • Evaluation and learning.
  • Stakeholder engagement.
  • Supporting advocacy initiatives.
  • Working with civil society.
  • Working with governments.
  • Working with international partners.

6. Communication and Organizational Skills

Strong communication, writing, organization and coordination skills are essential.

Candidates should have experience planning and delivering:

  • Meetings.
  • Workshops.
  • Events.
  • Stakeholder engagements.
  • Other programme activities.

7. Ability to Work Remotely

Because this is a remote-first position, applicants must be capable of working independently.

This includes:

  • Managing competing priorities.
  • Taking initiative.
  • Meeting deadlines.
  • Maintaining attention to detail.
  • Working effectively without constant direct supervision.

8. Digital Communications Skills

Candidates must demonstrate proficiency in digital communications tools and platforms, including social media.

9. Ability to Travel

The successful candidate must be able to undertake travel throughout the Balkans and wider Europe when required.

10. English Language

Fluency in English, both written and spoken, is mandatory.

All applications must also be submitted in English.

11. Commitment to IDC’s Mission and Values

Candidates must demonstrate a strong commitment to IDC’s mission and values, including its safeguarding and child protection principles.

Desirable Qualifications and Additional Skills

In addition to the essential criteria, IDC identifies several desirable qualifications.

These include:

  • Experience working within networks or coalitions.
  • Experience facilitating collaboration between diverse member organizations.
  • Experience facilitating peer learning.
  • Knowledge of immigration detention in the Western Balkans.
  • Knowledge of rights-based alternatives to immigration detention.
  • Proficiency in Serbian and/or Albanian.
  • Experience with regional cooperation mechanisms.

Knowledge of Serbian or Albanian is described as a strong asset, rather than a mandatory requirement.

Where Is the Job Based?

The role is described as remote and IDC operates as a remote-first organization.

However, the job has a specific geographic eligibility requirement.

Candidates must already have the legal right to reside and work in one of the following locations:

  1. Albania
  2. Bosnia and Herzegovina
  3. Greece
  4. Kosovo
  5. Montenegro
  6. North Macedonia
  7. Serbia

IDC states that it cannot sponsor work permits or support relocation.

This means that being interested in the role or being willing to relocate to one of these countries does not, based on the supplied job description, satisfy the requirement. Applicants must already possess the relevant legal right to reside and work.

Salary and Contract

The Europe Programme Officer – Balkans position is a full-time role.

The advertised compensation is

EUR 30,000 to EUR 40,000 per year, depending on the candidate’s location and experience.

The initial contract duration is one year, with the possibility of extension depending on funding.

The role currently has no direct reports, although interns or volunteers may report to the position where relevant.

Who Should Consider Applying?

This position may be relevant to professionals with backgrounds in areas such as

  • Migration and refugee affairs.
  • Human rights.
  • International relations.
  • Political science.
  • Law.
  • Migration studies.
  • Social sciences.
  • Advocacy.
  • Programme management.
  • Policy engagement.
  • Civil society programming.
  • Regional cooperation.
  • Communications and public information.

However, applicants should note that having a general background in these areas alone is not sufficient according to the stated criteria. IDC specifically requires relevant professional experience, including experience connected to migration and/or human rights and the Balkans.

Diversity, Inclusion and Lived Experience

IDC states that it values diversity, equality and inclusivity and welcomes applications from all backgrounds.

The organization specifically encourages applications from people from underrepresented backgrounds, including with regard to:

  • Gender.
  • Race.
  • Age.
  • Sexual orientation.
  • Disability.
  • Religion.

IDC also particularly encourages leaders with lived experience of the impacts of detention to apply.

Candidates who require adaptations to the usual recruitment process are encouraged to indicate this in their application.

Application Process

Applicants interested in the Europe Programme Officer – Balkans position must submit:

  • A resume/CV.
  • A cover letter.

Applications must be submitted through the IDC Careers webpage.

The deadline is

16 October 2026

Applicants should ensure that their application directly addresses the key selection criteria rather than relying on a generic CV and cover letter.

The organization specifically asks applicants to clearly address the requirements outlined in the vacancy.

Applications must be submitted in English.

Importantly, IDC states that applications sent by email will not be accepted. The advertised email address is provided for enquiries rather than application submission.

Only shortlisted candidates will be contacted, and the selected candidate is expected to start as soon as possible.

APPLY HERE

How to Strengthen Your Application

Applicants should ensure that their CV and cover letter clearly demonstrate evidence against the selection criteria.

A strong application should make it easy for the recruitment team to identify relevant experience in:

Migration and Human Rights

Explain specific responsibilities and projects involving migration, asylum, refugees, detention, human rights or related policy issues.

Balkans and European Policy

Highlight direct experience with the Balkans, Greece, EU institutions, EU accession, enlargement, migration policy or regional cooperation.

Advocacy

Demonstrate experience developing or implementing advocacy strategies, engaging policymakers, supporting campaigns or working with government and civil society stakeholders.

Programme Management

Show experience managing projects, timelines, deliverables, meetings, workshops, events and partnerships.

Research and Reporting

Highlight research, evidence gathering, reporting, monitoring, evaluation and learning experience.

Communications

Demonstrate experience preparing written materials, briefing notes, digital content, social media materials or strategic communications.

Stakeholder Engagement

Identify examples of working with governments, civil society organizations, UN agencies, international organizations, regional institutions or other networks.

Fundraising

Where applicable, demonstrate experience researching donors, contributing to funding proposals, coordinating proposal inputs or supporting donor reporting.

Remote Working

Show evidence that you can work independently, manage competing priorities and deliver work to deadlines.

Visit HERE for more information about the International Detention Coalition Europe Programme Officer position.

Important Deadline

The deadline to apply for the International Detention Coalition Europe Programme Officer – Balkans position is:

16 October 2026

Applicants should submit their CV and cover letter through the IDC Careers webpage before the deadline.

The organization states that applications sent by email will not be accepted.

Conclusion

The International Detention Coalition Europe Programme Officer – Balkans position provides an opportunity for an experienced migration, human rights, advocacy or programme professional to contribute to regional work across the Balkans and wider Europe.

The role combines programme management, advocacy, research, stakeholder engagement, communications, monitoring and evaluation, fundraising support and regional networking, making it particularly relevant to professionals who can work across both strategic and operational responsibilities.

The position requires a relevant university degree and at least three years of professional experience, together with demonstrated knowledge of migration, asylum, human rights and advocacy in the Balkans or relevant European contexts. Applicants must also have the legal right to reside and work in Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Greece, Kosovo, Montenegro, North Macedonia or Serbia, as IDC does not provide work-permit sponsorship or relocation support.

With a salary of EUR 30,000–40,000 annually, a full-time remote-first arrangement and an initial one-year contract with possible extension, the position is structured for an experienced professional who can contribute independently while working closely with regional and international stakeholders.

The application deadline is 16 October 2026, and applicants are required to submit their CV and cover letter through the IDC Careers webpage in English.

item.content:encoded:
Applications are open for the AI Entrepreneurs Lab 2026, an intensive founder programme designed to help promising Master’s and PhD-level talent transform applied artificial intelligence and robotics ideas into credible early-stage ventures.

Organized by 28DIGITAL under the EIT Community AI & Robotics and positioned within the EU ApplyAI Strategy, the AI Entrepreneurs Lab is aimed at technically capable students and graduates who are ready to move beyond research, prototypes and demonstrations and begin testing whether their ideas can become viable companies.

The programme takes a distinctly practical approach. Participants are not being invited to spend five days simply learning entrepreneurship theory. Instead, selected founders are expected to work intensively on their ideas, engage with customers and market actors, test assumptions, receive feedback from entrepreneurs, investors and companies, develop a stronger commercial model and gather evidence that their concept could become a real venture.

Up to 15 participants will join the cohort. Applications may be submitted individually or as a team of up to two people, and candidates may apply with either an early-stage concept or a recently incorporated startup that remains at the pre-launch stage.

The programme culminates in a Demo Day, where participants will present the progress and evidence they have generated. Up to five prizes of €10,000 each will be awarded on merit to teams demonstrating the strongest evidence of venture potential. The funding is intended to support concrete next steps in developing the company.

The five-day in-person bootcamp is scheduled for 9–13 November 2026, with activities taking place across three cities. Awards are connected with the EU Apply AI Summit in Brussels.

Applications opened on 1 September 2026 at 09:00 CET and close on 21 October 2026 at 17:00 CET.

About the AI Entrepreneurs Lab 2026

The AI Entrepreneurs Lab has been created around a straightforward challenge: Europe has substantial artificial intelligence research and technical talent, but promising research does not automatically become a sustainable company.

The programme therefore seeks to help technically strong graduate talent move from what it describes as the “lab bench to the founder’s seat.”

Its emphasis is on applied AI and robotics businesses that can ultimately be:

  • Trusted
  • Deployed
  • Commercialized
  • Scaled
  • Tested against genuine user or customer needs

The programme is consequently not focused primarily on producing polished presentations.

The organizers explicitly emphasize that participants should be “judged on evidence, not slides.”

This means applicants should be prepared to investigate whether their proposed solution addresses an actual problem, whether potential users or customers value it, whether the underlying technology is credible and whether there is a realistic path from technical concept to market.

Who Organizes the AI Entrepreneurs Lab?

The programme operates under the EIT Community AI & Robotics and is delivered by 28DIGITAL.

It is also presented as part of the wider EU ApplyAI Strategy.

This positioning connects the Lab to European efforts to increase the practical deployment and commercialization of artificial intelligence technologies rather than limiting AI development to experimentation and research.

For participants, this means the programme sits at the intersection of:

  • AI research
  • Robotics
  • Entrepreneurship
  • Commercialization
  • European innovation
  • Startup development
  • Investment readiness

How Many Participants Will Be Selected?

The programme is designed as a small and intensive cohort.

Up to:

15 people

will participate.

This is important because the official programme language refers to a 15-strong cohort, rather than 15 separate companies.

Since applicants may apply alone or in teams of up to two people, the final number of ventures represented could therefore be lower than the total number of participants.

AI Entrepreneurs Lab 2026 Programme Dates

The five-day founder bootcamp is scheduled for:

9–13 November 2026

The programme is conducted in person.

According to the call, it runs across:

Three cities in five days

and culminates in a Demo Day.

Applicants should therefore make sure they can participate fully in an intensive multi-day, in-person programme before applying.

Who Is the Programme Designed For?

The AI Entrepreneurs Lab targets Master’s and PhD students and graduates who have strong ideas involving artificial intelligence or robotics and want to investigate whether those ideas can become viable companies.

Candidates can apply:

  • Individually; or
  • As a team of up to two people.

Applications are submitted in the applicants’ personal capacity.

You do not need to have an established startup.

The programme accepts candidates who have:

  • An early-stage idea; or
  • A recently incorporated startup that is still at the pre-launch stage.

The key requirement is that AI or robotics must genuinely form the core of the proposed venture.

AI or Robotics Must Be Central to the Business

One of the clearest requirements in the call is that artificial intelligence or robotics should not simply be added to an otherwise unrelated business concept for branding purposes.

The organizers want ideas where AI or robotics is:

Genuinely central to what is being built.

That could mean the proposed technology is fundamental to:

  • The product
  • The service
  • The business model
  • The technical architecture
  • The user’s value proposition

Applicants should therefore be able to explain why the venture could not reasonably operate in the same way without its AI or robotics component.

What Makes a Strong Applicant?

The programme provides several indicators of what it considers a strong fit.

1. A Real Problem

Applicants should be able to identify a meaningful problem.

A technically sophisticated idea alone is unlikely to be enough.

Candidates should be prepared to explain:

  • Who experiences the problem
  • Why it matters
  • How the problem is currently addressed
  • Why existing solutions are insufficient
  • Who might ultimately pay for or adopt the solution

2. A Credible Technical Direction

Applicants are not necessarily expected to arrive with a finished product.

However, they should have a plausible technical direction.

That could involve:

  • A research concept
  • A technical prototype
  • A clearly defined architecture
  • Early experimentation
  • Relevant research expertise
  • A defensible technological hypothesis

The organisers want evidence that the AI or robotics component is technically meaningful rather than superficial.

3. A Plausible Path to Market

The Lab is fundamentally entrepreneurship-focused.

Participants should therefore be able to begin answering questions such as:

  • Who would use this?
  • Who would buy it?
  • What market does it address?
  • What problem does it solve better than existing alternatives?
  • What is the route to deployment?
  • What barriers might prevent adoption?

Applicants do not need to have all of these questions solved before applying, but they should demonstrate that they are thinking beyond the technology itself.

Priority Technology Areas

The call highlights a number of areas under Core AI and Robotics.

These include:

AI Agents and Autonomous Systems

Ideas involving systems capable of carrying out tasks or making decisions with varying levels of autonomy may fit within the programme.

This could potentially include applications involving:

  • Autonomous agents
  • Multi-agent systems
  • Decision-support systems
  • Workflow automation
  • Autonomous planning

The venture should still be built around a real user or market problem.

Edge AI and AI Infrastructure

The programme is also interested in technologies supporting the infrastructure on which AI systems operate.

This may include areas such as:

  • Edge computing
  • AI deployment infrastructure
  • Distributed AI
  • Model-serving infrastructure
  • Resource-efficient AI systems

Robotics Intelligence

Robotics is explicitly included.

Relevant ventures could focus on the intelligence layer behind robotic systems, rather than merely conventional mechanical design.

Potential areas may include:

  • Autonomous navigation
  • Robot perception
  • Human-robot interaction
  • Robotic decision-making
  • Industrial robotics intelligence

The call itself does not limit applicants to particular industries.

Trustworthy and Secure AI

Applicants working on AI safety, security and trust may also fit particularly well.

This category reflects the programme’s emphasis on building technologies that can be responsibly deployed.

Relevant questions could involve:

  • AI security
  • Model reliability
  • Transparency
  • Safety
  • Verification
  • Risk management
  • Responsible deployment

Foundation and Generative Models

The Lab welcomes ideas involving foundation models and generative AI.

This could include technologies built around:

  • Large language models
  • Generative systems
  • Multimodal models
  • Domain-specific foundation models

However, the requirement that AI be genuinely central remains important.

Simply adding a generic chatbot interface to an otherwise conventional product would not automatically demonstrate the level of technical centrality described in the call.

Industrial AI Deployment

Projects concerned with deploying AI in industrial environments are another explicit area of interest.

Such ventures might focus on applying AI to practical operational problems and overcoming the gap between technical experimentation and real-world deployment.

Be Ready to Test the Idea Publicly

The programme is not designed for participants who want to keep every part of their business thinking private while developing the idea in isolation.

Successful applicants should be willing to test their assumptions with:

  • Customers
  • Founders
  • Investors
  • Mentors
  • Companies

The Lab describes this as testing the idea “in public.”

The objective is to use external evidence to challenge assumptions and improve the venture quickly.

What Happens During the Five-Day Bootcamp?

The programme is designed as a practical founder-development experience.

While the exact daily schedule is not included in the information provided, the official call identifies several core areas of work.

Participants will receive support around:

  • Founder readiness
  • Customer discovery
  • Commercial-model testing
  • Pitch development
  • Investor readiness

These areas represent some of the main obstacles faced by technical founders attempting to convert research or prototypes into businesses.

Founder Readiness

Moving from researcher or student to startup founder requires a different set of responsibilities.

Participants may need to develop their ability to:

  • Make decisions with incomplete information
  • Communicate a clear business proposition
  • Prioritize work
  • Speak with customers
  • Respond to market feedback
  • Explain technical ideas to nontechnical stakeholders

The Lab is structured specifically around this transition from technical talent to founder.

Customer Discovery

One of the programme’s most important components is customer discovery.

Participants will be expected to test whether the problem they believe exists is genuinely important to the people or organizations they expect to serve.

This can help founders determine whether they need to:

  • Refine the product
  • Change the target customer
  • Reframe the problem
  • Change the business model
  • Adjust the technical solution

The emphasis on customer discovery is consistent with the programme’s broader focus on evidence rather than assumptions.

Commercial Model Testing

A technically impressive technology does not automatically create a sustainable company.

The programme therefore includes commercial-model testing.

Participants may need to examine issues such as:

  • Who pays
  • Pricing
  • Distribution
  • Business-to-business versus consumer models
  • Licensing
  • Partnerships
  • Market access

The purpose is to move closer to a venture that could operate beyond the bootcamp.

Pitch Development

Participants will also work on how they communicate their venture.

A strong pitch must explain both:

  • What the technology does; and
  • Why it should exist as a company.

Participants should therefore expect to refine how they communicate:

  • The problem
  • Their solution
  • Technical differentiation
  • Target users
  • Market opportunity
  • Evidence generated
  • Next steps

Investor Readiness

The programme also includes investor-readiness support.

Not every early-stage startup is immediately ready for institutional investment, but founders should understand how investors evaluate ventures.

The Lab can help participants begin developing the evidence and communication skills required for future fundraising.

A Cohort, Not a Classroom

The organizers describe the Lab as:

“A cohort, not a classroom.”

This language reflects the programme’s emphasis on interaction and practical work rather than conventional lectures.

Participants will join a small group of other technically oriented founders working on applied AI and robotics ventures.

That cohort structure can potentially create opportunities for:

  • Peer feedback
  • Collaboration
  • Knowledge exchange
  • Future partnerships
  • Founder networks

Hands-On Mentoring

The selected participants will receive mentoring from people with experience in:

  • Founding companies
  • Scaling companies
  • Deploying technologies
  • Commercialization
  • Investment

Rather than focusing solely on academic theory, mentoring is intended to help participants make concrete progress on their ventures.

Direct Market Contact

The Lab also provides opportunities for direct interaction with:

  • Mentors
  • Startups
  • Corporates
  • Investors

Participants can use these conversations to test assumptions and gather feedback.

The programme also highlights introductions that may continue to be valuable after the five-day experience ends.

Demo Day

The programme concludes with a Demo Day.

This is where participants demonstrate what they have learned and the evidence they have generated about their venture during the programme.

The selection of prize winners is based on demonstrated venture progress rather than simply the visual quality of a presentation.

The official programme language emphasizes awarding the teams that show the:

Strongest evidence of a real venture.

Up to Five €10,000 Prizes

One of the major components of the AI Entrepreneurs Lab is its financial award structure.

Up to:

Five prizes

will be awarded.

Each prize is worth:

€10,000

This means up to €50,000 in total prizes could potentially be distributed if all five awards are made.

The funding is intended to support concrete venture progress after the programme.

Importantly, the €10,000 should not be described as guaranteed funding for every participant.

It is a competitive prize awarded on merit at Demo Day.

EU Apply AI Summit in Brussels

The programme’s awards are connected with the EU Apply AI Summit in Brussels.

This adds a broader European innovation context to the programme and can potentially expose selected founders to a wider network involved in the European AI ecosystem.

Travel and Accommodation Support

The programme states that travel and accommodation assistance for the selected Top 15 may be provided.

However, this support is:

Subject to programme rules and available budget.

Applicants should therefore not assume that all travel and accommodation costs are automatically fully funded.

The correct interpretation is that support may be available, depending on applicable rules and budget.

Applicants for whom travel support is essential should confirm the applicable conditions before making commitments.

How to Apply

Candidates must submit one application through the official platform before the deadline.

Applicants are required to provide:

  1. A completed application form
  2. A CV for each team member
  3. A short, creative presentation of the proposed idea

If applying as a two-person team, both team members should therefore prepare individual CVs.

Apply here:
AI Entrepreneurs Lab Application Form

What Should the Idea Presentation Show?

The source does not prescribe a specific slide count or exact format for the creative presentation in the information provided.

Applicants should therefore avoid assuming requirements that have not been stated.

However, based directly on the published selection profile, the presentation should clearly communicate the elements the programme says it values:

  • The problem
  • The proposed solution
  • Why AI or robotics is central
  • Technical direction
  • Target customer or user
  • Potential path to market
  • Current stage of development

Candidates should follow any additional instructions presented in the application platform.

Can You Apply Without a Startup?

Yes.

Applicants can participate with an early concept.

You do not need to have incorporated a company before applying.

The programme is specifically designed to help turn:

Research and raw ideas into the foundations of a company.

Can an Existing Startup Apply?

Yes, but the opportunity targets very early-stage ventures.

A recently incorporated startup may apply if it remains at:

Pre-launch stage.

The Lab is therefore not aimed at mature companies with established operations and substantial commercial traction.

Can You Apply Alone?

Yes.

Candidates may apply as:

  • A solo founder; or
  • A team of up to two people.

Solo applicants therefore do not need to find a co-founder before submitting an application.

Application Timeline

The application window opened on:

1 September 2026 at 09:00 CET

and closes on:

21 October 2026 at 17:00 CET

Applicants should note the precise closing time.

This is not a deadline that simply runs until midnight on October 21.

Final deadline: 21 October 2026 at 17:00 CET.

Programme Timeline

Key dates include:

Applications open: 1 September 2026, 09:00 CET

Application deadline: 21 October 2026, 17:00 CET

Five-day in-person bootcamp: 9–13 November 2026

Participants should ensure they can attend the full in-person programme before applying.

How to Prepare a Strong Application

Applicants should focus on demonstrating that they have more than an interesting technical concept.

Explain the Problem First

Do not begin with a long explanation of model architecture without explaining why the technology is needed.

Make clear:

  • Who experiences the problem
  • How serious the problem is
  • Why existing solutions are insufficient

Demonstrate Why AI or Robotics Is Essential

The programme explicitly rejects ideas where AI appears to be added merely as a fashionable label.

Applicants should explain:

  • What the AI or robotics component actually does
  • Why it is necessary
  • What technical advantage it creates
  • Why the venture would be substantially different without it

Show Technical Credibility

Applicants should demonstrate that they understand how the proposed technology might actually be built.

Relevant evidence might include:

  • Academic research
  • Master’s thesis work
  • PhD research
  • Prototype development
  • Technical experiments
  • Previous AI or robotics projects

Demonstrate Commercial Curiosity

Applicants do not need a complete business plan.

However, they should show that they are already thinking about:

  • Customers
  • Users
  • Markets
  • Deployment
  • Competition
  • Pricing
  • Adoption

The programme is specifically designed to move technical talent toward company creation.

Be Open to Changing Your Idea

Because the Lab emphasizes customer feedback and evidence, strong participants should be willing to discover that some of their initial assumptions are wrong.

The purpose of the five days is not simply to prove that the original idea was perfect.

It is to determine what evidence supports a viable venture and adapt accordingly.

Key Information at a Glance

Programme: AI Entrepreneurs Lab 2026

Organizer: 28DIGITAL under the EIT Community AI & Robotics

Strategic context: EU ApplyAI Strategy

Focus: Applied artificial intelligence and robotics entrepreneurship

Target group: Master’s and PhD students and graduates

Applicant format: Solo applicants or teams of up to two

Venture stage: Early concept or recently incorporated pre-launch startup

Cohort size: Up to 15 participants

Format: Five-day in-person founder bootcamp

Bootcamp dates: 9–13 November 2026

Structure: Three cities in five days, concluding with Demo Day

Funding opportunity: Up to five €10,000 prizes

Prize basis: Merit at Demo Day

Potential travel/accommodation support: May be available subject to programme rules and budget

Application requirements: Application form, CV for each team member and short creative presentation of the idea

Applications opened: 1 September 2026 at 09:00 CET

Deadline: 21 October 2026 at 17:00 CET

Official programme page:    AI Entrepreneurs Lab

APPLY HERE

Conclusion

The AI Entrepreneurs Lab 2026 offers Master’s and PhD-level AI and robotics talent an opportunity to explore one of the most difficult transitions in technological innovation: moving from technically promising research or an early idea toward a company capable of solving a genuine market problem.

Rather than functioning as a conventional entrepreneurship course, the Lab is built around practical experimentation. Participants are expected to test assumptions with customers, receive feedback from founders and investors, refine their commercial models and develop evidence that their technology could become a viable venture.

Up to 15 participants will join the intensive five-day programme, with applicants able to participate individually or in teams of two. Ideas may still be at concept stage, while recently incorporated pre-launch startups are also eligible.

The programme is particularly suited to candidates working in areas including AI agents and autonomous systems, edge AI and infrastructure, robotics intelligence, trustworthy and secure AI, foundation and generative models and industrial AI deployment.

At the conclusion of the Lab, participants will present their progress at Demo Day. Up to five ventures can receive €10,000 each to support concrete next steps.

Candidates should remember that the €10,000 is a competitive prize rather than guaranteed funding and that travel and accommodation support, while potentially available for the Top 15, is subject to programme rules and budget.

For technically strong Master’s and PhD students or graduates who have begun asking not only “Can this technology work?” but also “Can this become a company?”, the programme provides an opportunity to test that question intensively.

Applications close on 21 October 2026 at 17:00 CET.

item.content:encoded:
Coefficient Giving has opened a major funding opportunity for individuals, fund managers, philanthropic organizations, regrantors, incubators, and implementing organizations with ambitious ideas for tackling important and underfunded problems in global health and wellbeing.

Through its Launchpad Funds Request for Proposals (RFP), Coefficient Giving is accepting Expressions of Interest (EOIs) from applicants who believe they can develop or scale a fund capable of generating substantial, measurable impact and eventually deploying $100 million or more in philanthropic capital.

The initiative has two funding tracks: pre-seed funding ranging from $200,000 to $10 million over up to 24 months, and seed and scaling funding ranging from $10 million to $50 million or more over up to 36 months. For exceptional proposals, Coefficient Giving may consider funding above $50 million.

The deadline for Expressions of Interest is October 2, 2026, with applications evaluated on a rolling basis.

About the Coefficient Giving Launchpad Funds Opportunity

The Launchpad Funds initiative has been designed to help create and strengthen funds capable of addressing some of the world’s most significant and underfunded challenges in global health and well-being.

Coefficient Giving explains that it is increasing its giving partly in anticipation of billions of dollars in potentially available philanthropic capital in the coming years. The organization wants to help develop an ecosystem of regrantors and implementers that can allocate this future funding effectively and cost-effectively.

Rather than simply funding individual projects, the Launchpad Funds model focuses on developing funds that can identify, support, and scale multiple initiatives working toward a common objective.

The organization is therefore looking for proposals that demonstrate a clear understanding of a major problem, a credible pathway toward solving or reducing it, and the potential to attract and deploy significant additional funding.

The ultimate ambition is for selected Launchpad Funds to grow into organizations capable of deploying $100 million or more over the next several years, with the strongest proposals potentially reaching $300 million or more in philanthropic deployment over three to five years.

What Funding Is Available?

Coefficient Giving has established two separate application tracks.

1. Pre-Seed Funding: $200,000 to $10 Million

The pre-seed track is designed for new fund concepts that require support to develop their strategy, establish an operating structure, build a team, and potentially begin exploratory grantmaking.

Funding can be provided for a period of up to 24 months.

Depending on the level of funding required, support may be used for:

  • Developing the initial fund concept and strategy.
  • Researching and defining the problem the fund intends to address.
  • Supporting an individual applicant while they develop the fund idea.
  • Building a founding team.
  • Developing the operational infrastructure required to establish the fund.
  • Conducting initial exploratory grantmaking at the highest funding levels.
  • Identifying and recruiting an appropriate general manager where the original idea generator does not intend to manage the fund.

An important point for applicants is that pre-seed funding does not automatically guarantee subsequent seed or scaling funding. The purpose of this stage is to develop, test, learn about, and de-risk the proposed fund before larger-scale deployment.

Coefficient Giving also recognizes that the person who develops an excellent fund concept may not necessarily be the best person to manage it. Consequently, applicants who have strong ideas but do not intend to become fund managers are also encouraged to apply.

2. Seed and Scaling Funding: $10 Million to $50 Million+

The second track is intended for more developed ideas that are ready to establish or significantly expand a fund.

Funding ranges from $10 million to $50 million or more for up to 36 months. Exceptional proposals may be considered for funding beyond $50 million.

This track is particularly relevant to:

  • Established funds that have significant potential to scale.
  • Funds that have developed strong strategies but have not yet secured sufficient anchor funding.
  • Existing initiatives that could substantially expand beyond their current funding level.
  • Fund concepts with evidence of potential impact and a credible pathway toward much larger capital deployment.

While some funding may cover operating expenses, Coefficient Giving expects most of the funding to support activities directly contributing to the fund’s objectives, including regranting or direct implementation.

Selected proposals may potentially receive further funding after the initial grant period, although additional funding is not guaranteed.

What Is a Launchpad Fund?

The central concept behind this opportunity is the creation or expansion of a Launchpad Fund.

A Launchpad Fund is primarily intended to function as a regrantor, providing financial support to initiatives and projects led by implementing organizations that are working toward the fund’s overall objectives.

However, Coefficient Giving is also open to situations where an implementing organization is itself best positioned to take responsibility for an entire problem and effectively fill the role of a general manager.

This means applicants do not necessarily need to have an existing traditional grantmaking organization. What matters is whether they have a compelling idea, credible strategy, and the capacity or potential to develop a mechanism capable of directing substantial resources toward an important problem.

Who Can Apply?

Coefficient Giving has intentionally opened the opportunity to several categories of applicants.

Eligible applicant types identified in the RFP include:

Individuals

Individuals who are well-positioned to become a general manager for a particular issue area can apply.

If selected, successful individual applicants would be expected to treat developing and managing the initiative as a full-time job.

Importantly, individuals do not necessarily need to already have the organizational structure needed to host a fund. Coefficient Giving states that it is more interested in the strength of the idea than the applicant’s existing ability to host a fund and will work with selected applicants to determine an appropriate organizational arrangement.

Early-Stage Funds

Early-stage funds with established founding teams are also eligible to submit proposals.

This category may be particularly relevant to teams that have already developed a strong concept but require significant funding to move from an early-stage idea toward a functioning and scalable fund.

Existing Funds

Existing funds with substantial potential for growth can apply for seed and scaling support.

The opportunity is therefore not limited to newly created organizations. Existing initiatives can seek funding if they can demonstrate a credible opportunity to expand their reach, funding capacity, and impact.

Philanthropic Funders, Regrantors and Incubators

Philanthropic funders, regrantors, and incubators can apply with concepts for funds they could host.

This includes existing foundation programs that have the potential to be significantly expanded.

Implementing Organizations

Organizations that are directly implementing programs can also apply if they have a strong vision for tackling a major problem.

In some circumstances, an implementing organization may take responsibility for an entire problem rather than focusing on a narrow component of it.

What Types of Problems Will the Coefficient Giving Fund Solve?

The RFP focuses broadly on global health and well-being, particularly problems that are important but comparatively underfunded.

Coefficient Giving is not restricting applications to a single disease, intervention, country, or approach. The organization specifically states that it wants to surface ideas that its team may not have encountered previously.

Potential areas include:

  • Diseases that create particularly large burdens in specific regions.
  • Environmental risk factors that contribute to health problems.
  • Areas that are structurally neglected by existing philanthropic funding programs.
  • Important but highly specialized problems requiring exceptional expertise.
  • Initiatives aimed at accelerating the deployment or uptake of technologies with strong evidence behind them.
  • Other important and underfunded global health and well-being challenges.

One example identified in the RFP is malaria in Nigeria, illustrating the type of region-specific disease burden that could potentially be addressed through a targeted fund. Environmental risk reduction, such as improving air quality, is another example provided.

Applicants are not restricted to these examples. The list is explicitly described as illustrative rather than exhaustive.

What Makes a Strong Proposal?

Coefficient Giving places considerable emphasis on cost-effectiveness.

The organization states that cost-effectiveness will be the top consideration when assessing proposals. In practice, it expects promising proposals to perform strongly against its ITN framework: Importance, Tractability, and Neglectedness.

Importance

Applicants should demonstrate that the problem they want to address is sufficiently large and severe.

A strong proposal should explain:

  • How significant the problem is.
  • How many people or communities are affected?
  • What consequences the problem creates.
  • How much of the problem the proposed fund could plausibly address.

Tractability

The applicant should demonstrate that there is a credible pathway to achieving meaningful results.

This involves explaining:

  • Why the proposed strategy could work.
  • What evidence supports the interventions likely to be funded.
  • What bottlenecks currently prevent progress.
  • How the proposed fund could overcome those barriers.

Neglectedness

Applicants should show that the problem receives insufficient attention or funding relative to its importance.

The proposal should identify whether:

  • Existing funders are overlooking the issue.
  • Current funding is inadequate.
  • Important opportunities remain unaddressed.
  • The proposed fund would have a distinctive advantage in making progress.

Outcome-Oriented Funds Are Encouraged

Coefficient Giving indicates a preference for funds that are outcome-oriented.

This means that a strong fund should ideally be organized around a clearly defined objective or target rather than simply distributing money within a broad thematic area.

For example, a fund might be established around achieving a specific reduction in lead exposure or accelerating development of a particular health intervention.

However, thematic funds are not excluded.

A fund can be organized around a promising intervention or broad area even where there is not yet a fully quantified target. In such cases, the proposal should still have a clearly identifiable leader who is accountable for the fund’s direction.

General Manager Leadership

Coefficient Giving places importance on general manager-led funds.

The idea is that a particular individual should have clear responsibility for achieving the fund’s intended outcome.

Applicants should therefore consider who will be responsible for:

  • Setting the fund’s direction.
  • Developing its strategy.
  • Making strategic decisions.
  • Building relationships with relevant stakeholders.
  • Coordinating grantmaking or implementation.
  • Tracking progress toward the fund’s objectives.
  • Adjusting the strategy as evidence develops.

For individual applicants, being able to explain why they are particularly well-positioned to lead the proposed fund will be important.

The Scale of Ambition

A distinctive feature of the Launchpad Funds opportunity is the scale of funding and impact being contemplated.

Coefficient Giving is seeking funds that could eventually cost-effectively allocate at least $100 million, with a preference for proposals that could potentially deploy $300 million or more over three to five years.

The organization provides illustrative examples to demonstrate the scale of impact it is seeking.

At its stated 1,000x bar, Coefficient Giving indicates that a $100 million fund could, counterfactually:

  • Avert approximately 1 million disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) based on its stated valuation of $100,000 per DALY.
  • Correspond to approximately 20,000 under-five deaths averted or approximately 32,000 deaths among people over five.
  • Alternatively, increase annual income for approximately 2.1 million individuals by 10% for 10 years, based on its stated model of the utility of income.

These figures are presented by Coefficient Giving as illustrations of the scale of impact it is seeking rather than as guaranteed outcomes for applicants.

How Proposals Will Be Evaluated

Across both funding tracks, Coefficient Giving says proposals will be assessed using several major considerations.

1. The Problem

Applicants will need to demonstrate how their proposed problem performs against the Importance, Tractability and Neglectedness framework.

2. Cost-Effectiveness

The organization will assess whether the proposed fund can generate substantial impact relative to the amount of funding deployed.

3. Personnel

Coefficient Giving will consider whether the individual or team has the:

  • Track record.
  • Judgment.
  • Relevant expertise.
  • Networks.
  • Capacity required to achieve the proposed outcome.

4. Strategy

Applicants will need to demonstrate that their proposed approach is plausible and capable of addressing the identified problem.

5. Growth Pathway

A critical consideration is whether there is a realistic pathway from the initial Coefficient Giving grant to a $100 million-plus Launchpad Fund.

This means applicants should think beyond the immediate grant. They should explain how their initial funding could help establish the foundations for much larger-scale funding and impact.

Application Requirements for the Pre-Seed Track

Applicants applying for pre-seed funding must submit a short Expression of Interest.

The application requires:

  1. A resume or LinkedIn profile link.
  2. A 1,000-word proposal explaining:
    • The specific outcome or topic the proposed fund would own.
    • How the concept performs against the ITN framework.
    • Why the concept could become a $100 million-plus idea.
    • The key uncertainties that would need to be resolved during the scoping phase.
  3. A 300-word explanation of why the applicant is well-positioned to scope the proposed fund.
  4. A rough budget range and a short explanation of how the funding would be used.

Coefficient Giving estimates that completing the initial EOI should take approximately one to two hours.

Applicants who progress beyond the EOI stage may be asked to submit a more detailed proposal describing the initial fund strategy.

The organization may also request preliminary cost-effectiveness estimates or other supporting materials and may engage applicants in discussions and revisions.

Application Requirements for the Seed and Scaling Track

Applicants seeking seed and scaling funding must also submit a short Expression of Interest.

The application requires:

  1. Resumes or LinkedIn links for core team members.
  2. A 1,000-word fund proposal explaining:
    • The specific outcome or topic the fund would own.
    • How the proposal performs against the ITN framework.
    • Why the idea could become a $100 million-plus fund.
    • A rough timeline for achieving the fund’s goals.
  3. A 300-word explanation of why the head of the team is well-positioned to serve as general manager.
  4. A rough budget range and explanation of how the funding would be used.
  5. Existing fund materials, where applicable, including materials that already explain the fund’s strategy or demonstrate its impact. Existing funds do not need to create new materials solely for the application.

As with the pre-seed track, the initial EOI is expected to take approximately one to two hours to complete.

Applicants who advance will receive requests for additional materials tailored to their individual proposals.

Important Dates and Deadline

The deadline for submitting Expressions of Interest for both funding tracks is October 2, 2026.

However, the expected final decision timelines differ between the two tracks:

Pre-Seed Track

  • EOI deadline: October 2, 2026
  • Decision-making: Rolling basis
  • Target date for final decisions: December 15, 2026

Seed and Scaling Track

  • EOI deadline: October 2, 2026
  • Decision-making: Rolling basis
  • Target date for final decisions: May 1, 2027

Coefficient Giving may also make smaller grants to promising seed and scaling applicants earlier in the process while continuing to assess their suitability for larger funding amounts.

How to Apply

Applicants can submit an Expression of Interest through the Coefficient Giving application form provided in the RFP.

The same application link is used for both the pre-seed and seed and scaling tracks.

Applicants should prepare their materials carefully, particularly the description of the problem, the proposed fund strategy, the ITN analysis, expected impact, budget requirements, and pathway toward significant future scale.

The application should clearly demonstrate why the proposed fund represents an opportunity to address an important problem that is currently insufficiently funded.

APPLY HERE

What Applicants Should Consider Before Applying

Although the initial EOI is relatively short, the opportunity is highly ambitious. Applicants should therefore consider several issues before submitting.

Clearly Define the Problem

Avoid describing a broad challenge without identifying what the proposed fund would specifically seek to change.

Applicants should be able to explain what outcome the fund would ultimately own.

Demonstrate Why the Problem Matters

A proposal should provide a strong rationale for why the issue deserves significant philanthropic attention.

This includes considering its scale, severity, affected populations, and potential consequences.

Explain Why the Problem Is Tractable

Applicants should identify the interventions, technologies, policies, research, implementation approaches, or other mechanisms through which meaningful progress could potentially be achieved.

Demonstrate Neglectedness

Applicants should explain why existing funding mechanisms are not already adequately addressing the problem.

Think Beyond the Initial Grant

The RFP is specifically designed around funds that could eventually deploy very large amounts of philanthropic capital.

Applicants should therefore explain how the proposed fund could grow beyond the initial Coefficient Giving investment.

Identify the Right Leadership

Applicants should clearly establish who would be accountable for delivering the fund’s objectives and why that person or team is appropriately positioned to lead it.

Examples of Funds Supported by the Model

Coefficient Giving identifies several existing funds that fit the Launchpad model.

These include:

  • The Lead Exposure Action Fund, which aims to accelerate reductions in lead exposure.
  • The Strep A Vaccine Fund, which aims to accelerate development of a Strep A vaccine.
  • Renaissance Philanthropy’s Talent Mobility Fund, which focuses on expanding the use of existing immigration pathways to help people move to opportunities.

According to the RFP, these examples share characteristics such as addressing problems with substantial health or economic costs, receiving comparatively limited philanthropic funding, identifying bottlenecks preventing progress, and identifying potentially cost-effective ways to address those bottlenecks.

Additional Considerations for Applicants

Coefficient Giving expects most applicants to be individuals or nonprofit organizations. However, applicants with other organizational structures are encouraged to contact the organization if they believe their structure is appropriate for the opportunity.

Applicants should also be aware that Coefficient Giving may share application materials with other funders who could have an interest in the proposal.

If an applicant does not want their materials shared without prior consultation, this preference can be indicated in the Expression of Interest.

Because this is the first call for proposals of this type, the organization notes that it may not be able to move quickly on every proposal it finds interesting. Some proposals may be placed on hold for possible consideration at a later stage.

Due to the anticipated volume of submissions, Coefficient Giving also states that it will not be able to provide individualized feedback to applicants.

Frequently Relevant Questions

Can an individual apply without already having a fund?

Yes. The RFP specifically allows individuals who are well-positioned to become general managers for a particular issue area to apply. The organization states that it is more interested in the idea than the applicant’s existing ability to host a fund.

Does an applicant need to already have a large organization?

No specific requirement for an existing large organization is stated. The opportunity accepts individuals, early-stage funds, existing funds, philanthropic funders, regrantors, incubators, and implementing organizations.

Can an existing fund apply?

Yes. Existing funds with significant potential to scale can apply for the seed and scaling track.

Can an implementing organization apply?

Yes. Implementing organizations can apply if they have a vision for tackling a major problem, including through regranting to other organizations where appropriate.

Does receiving pre-seed funding guarantee future funding?

No. The RFP explicitly states that pre-seed funding is not a commitment to provide subsequent seed and scaling funding.

Can the proposed fund focus on an area not listed by Coefficient Giving?

Yes. The organization’s list of potentially promising areas is described as illustrative, and it states that it is open to proposals outside the listed areas.

Visit HERE for more information about the Coefficient Giving Launchpad Funds 2026.

Conclusion

The Coefficient Giving Launchpad Funds 2026 opportunity is designed for ambitious individuals and organizations seeking to build or scale funds capable of directing substantial philanthropic resources toward important and underfunded global health and wellbeing challenges.

With pre-seed funding of $200,000 to $10 million and seed and scaling funding of $10 million to $50 million or more, the initiative provides substantial potential support for both emerging fund concepts and established initiatives with significant scaling opportunities. The strongest proposals are expected to demonstrate a clear problem, credible strategy, strong leadership, cost-effective impact, and a realistic pathway toward developing a fund capable of deploying $100 million or more.

Applicants should pay particular attention to the Importance, Tractability and Neglectedness framework; clearly define the outcome they want their fund to achieve; explain why the issue is underfunded; and demonstrate how their proposed strategy could generate meaningful progress.

The Expression of Interest deadline for both tracks is October 2, 2026, and applications are reviewed on a rolling basis. Prospective applicants should therefore prepare their proposal materials early and ensure that their submission clearly communicates both the significance of the problem and the potential for the proposed fund to operate at substantial scale.
